title: WHEN DID BEING A CHRISTIAN BECOME MORE ABOUT WINNING ARGUMENTS THAN LOVING PEOPLE?
paragraphs: WHEN DID BEING A CHRISTIAN BECOME MORE ABOUT WINNING ARGUMENTS THAN LOVING PEOPLE?

We learned how to defend the truth, but somewhere along the way, some of us forgot how to love the very people Jesus died to save. And the most frightening part? We can be right about Scripture while being terribly wrong in the way we represent its Author.
He knew the Bible.

He could quote verses without opening it. He could recognize false teaching in seconds. He knew how to dismantle a theological argument, expose contradictions, and silence anyone who challenged his beliefs.
People called him bold.
Some called him a defender of the faith.
And perhaps, in many ways, he was.
But there was something nobody seemed to notice.
His wife had stopped telling him when she was hurting because every conversation became a lecture.
His children were afraid to ask difficult questions because curiosity was often mistaken for rebellion.
His struggling friend had stopped attending church because the last time he confessed his weakness, he received condemnation before compassion.

And somewhere on Facebook, a wounded stranger was reading another one of his perfectly constructed biblical arguments, wondering why the people who spoke most loudly about Jesus seemed so incapable of showing His kindness.
Then one evening, after another heated exchange, a question pierced the silence.
Not a question about whether his theology was correct.
Not a question about whether he had won.
Something far more uncomfortable.
"What if I've spent years defending Jesus in ways that make people afraid to come near Him?"
And suddenly, winning didn't feel much like victory anymore.
Perhaps that question is not just for him.
Perhaps it is for us.
Because somewhere between defending biblical truth and defending our own pride, something has gone terribly wrong.
We have become skilled at identifying what is wrong with the world while sometimes remaining strangely blind to what is wrong within ourselves.
We can recognize a false doctrine but overlook our own cruelty.
We can quote the command to repent while refusing to apologize.
We can expose someone else's sin publicly while protecting our own arrogance privately.
We can fight for the authority of Scripture while disobeying its clearest commands about how to treat people.
And then we wonder why some wounded people struggle to believe us when we say that God is love.
But before we point our fingers at other Christians, there is something we need to remember.
Jesus never called us to abandon truth for the sake of appearing loving.
And He never gave us permission to abandon love in the name of defending truth.
He embodied both perfectly.
The problem is not that Christians care too much about truth. The problem begins when we care more about proving ourselves right than representing Christ faithfully.
And Scripture has been warning us about this for nearly two thousand years.
The apostle Paul wrote to the Corinthians:
"Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal." — 1 Corinthians 13:1, KJV
Consider that.
A person can speak eloquently.
Understand theology.
Possess extraordinary knowledge.
Appear spiritually impressive.
And still become nothing more than noise when love is absent.
In 1 Corinthians 13:2, Paul goes even further. Even if he possessed all knowledge and extraordinary faith, without love, he says, "I am nothing."
Nothing.
Not slightly less effective.
Not simply in need of better communication skills.
Nothing.
The Greek word Paul uses for love is ἀγάπη (agapē).
In this passage, it describes the kind of love expressed through patience, kindness, humility, truthfulness, endurance, and self-giving concern for others.
It is not mere sentimentality.
It does not celebrate evil.
Paul explicitly says love "rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth" (1 Corinthians 13:6, KJV).
Biblical love and biblical truth are not enemies.
They belong together.
That means correcting someone can be an act of love.
Confronting destructive behavior can be an act of love.
Warning someone about sin can be an act of love.
But humiliating someone simply because we can?
Mocking their ignorance?
Enjoying their embarrassment?
Treating their brokenness as an opportunity to demonstrate our superiority?
We should never confuse those things with the fruit of the Holy Spirit.
Because the moment another person's humiliation becomes our satisfaction, we need to examine whose glory we are actually pursuing.
God's?
Or our own?
And here is where the Gospel becomes painfully personal.
There was once a man who knew the Scriptures, defended his religious convictions fiercely, and believed he was serving God.
His name was Saul.
Before he became known as the apostle Paul, he persecuted followers of Jesus.
Acts 8:3 describes him entering houses and dragging believers away to prison.
Acts 9:1 describes him as still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord.
Saul was not simply someone who enjoyed a heated theological debate.
He was a persecutor.
His story must not be reduced to ordinary disagreements between Christians.
But it reveals a terrifying possibility: religious certainty does not automatically mean spiritual faithfulness.
A person can sincerely believe he is defending God while acting against God's purposes.
Then, on the road to Damascus, Saul encountered the risen Christ.
And Jesus asked him:
"Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" — Acts 9:4, KJV
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not congratulate Saul for his zeal.
He did not praise his religious credentials.
He confronted him.
And in that confrontation, Jesus identified Himself with the very people Saul had been persecuting.
"Why persecutest thou me?"
Those words should unsettle anyone who claims to love Christ while treating His people with contempt.
Not because every criticism of another Christian is persecution.
Not because every disagreement is unloving.
But because Jesus takes our treatment of others seriously.
Saul had to discover that being zealous for God was not the same as knowing the heart of God.
And perhaps some of us need to discover that too.
Maybe you have never persecuted anyone.
Maybe you have never dragged a believer into prison.
But perhaps you have used Scripture like a weapon when it should have been a light.
Perhaps you have corrected people more quickly than you have prayed for them.
Perhaps someone once trusted you with a confession, and instead of helping them carry their burden toward Christ, you made them regret ever opening their heart.
Perhaps you have typed words online that you would be ashamed to say while looking into someone's tear-filled eyes.
Or perhaps you are the one who was wounded.
You asked an honest question and were treated like an enemy.
You admitted you were struggling and someone questioned whether your faith was real.
You walked into a church hoping to encounter grace and left feeling that your mistakes were the only things anyone could see.
If that is your story, please hear this.
The cruelty of a Christian is not an accurate portrait of the character of Christ.
Jesus does not become less holy because His followers sometimes fail to reflect His holiness.
And His invitation to come to Him remains open.
There is a moment in John's Gospel that deserves our attention.
Jesus had been teaching in the temple when religious leaders brought before Him a woman accused of adultery.
They placed her in the middle of the crowd.
Her shame became a public spectacle.
Her future hung in the balance.
They asked Jesus what should be done.
But John tells us their question was a test, intended to give them grounds for accusing Him.
Jesus answered:
"He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." — John 8:7, KJV
One by one, her accusers departed.
Then Jesus said:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." — John 8:11, KJV

The scene is preserved in John 7:53–8:11, a passage whose earliest manuscript status is disputed and which many modern Bibles identify with a textual note. It should therefore not be treated as the sole foundation for a doctrine. Yet its portrait of mercy joined to a call away from sin is consistent with teachings firmly attested elsewhere in Scripture.
And what a portrait it is.
Jesus did not declare adultery righteous.
He did not tell the woman that sin was harmless.
But neither did He allow her accusers to turn her suffering into an opportunity for self-righteousness.
He refused the false choice between holiness and mercy.
He showed that compassion does not require calling evil good.
And calling people to repentance does not require stripping them of dignity.
This is the Jesus we claim to follow.
The One who could speak with perfect moral authority and yet receive sinners.
The One who confronted hypocrisy without becoming hypocritical.
The One who exposed darkness while offering Himself as the light of the world.
The One who never needed to win an argument to satisfy His ego, because He had no sinful ego to defend.
Think about the people Jesus encountered.
Zacchaeus, a wealthy tax collector despised by many, found Jesus willing to enter his home. That encounter was followed by repentance expressed in restitution and generosity (Luke 19:1–10).
The Samaritan woman at the well was not ignored because of her complicated personal history. Jesus spoke truthfully with her about her life and revealed Himself as the Messiah (John 4:1–26).
Peter denied knowing Jesus three times. After the resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
None of these encounters required Jesus to compromise truth.
And none required Him to treat broken people as disposable.
That is the Gospel.
Not a soft message that pretends sin does not matter.
Not a harsh message that leaves sinners believing grace is beyond their reach.
The Gospel declares that sin is so serious that Christ went to the cross, and God's mercy is so astonishing that Christ willingly went there for sinners.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were still sinners.
Not after we mastered every doctrine.
Not after we corrected every bad habit.
Not after we became impressive enough to deserve His attention.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
And if that truth has truly taken root in our hearts, how can we look at another struggling human being as though we ourselves were rescued by personal superiority?
We were rescued by grace.
The Greek word χάρις (charis), translated "grace," speaks of favor or gift, and in Ephesians 2:8–9 Paul emphasizes that salvation is God's gift, not something earned through works.
This does not mean good works are irrelevant. The very next verse, Ephesians 2:10, says believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
But those works flow from grace.
They do not purchase it.
And this matters enormously when we speak about repentance, discipleship, and how we treat people who have not yet come to believe.
We do not stand above them as people who saved ourselves.
We stand before them as witnesses to the Savior who rescued us.
There is a difference.
A life-changing difference.
And it should be visible in our words.
James 1:19 instructs believers to be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to wrath.
Think about how radically that instruction challenges the way many of us behave online.
Someone posts an opinion we dislike.
Our fingers move before our hearts have listened.
We assume motives.
We construct arguments against things the person never actually said.
We interpret disagreement as hostility.
We deliver the final devastating reply.
And then we walk away feeling victorious.
But what if the person on the other side of that screen is grieving?
What if they are recovering from spiritual abuse?
What if they are asking clumsy questions because nobody ever patiently taught them?
What if they are an unbeliever trying to understand why Christians believe what they believe?
What if they are a brother or sister in Christ who is simply mistaken?
What if they are right about something we have overlooked?
We cannot know everything about someone's heart from a comment section.
And that is precisely why humility matters.
The apostle Peter wrote:
"But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear." — 1 Peter 3:15, KJV
The Greek word translated "answer" is ἀπολογία (apologia), meaning a defense or reasoned response.
It is related to the English word apologetics.
So yes, Christians are called to explain and defend their faith.
Christianity is not an invitation to intellectual laziness.
Questions deserve thoughtful answers.
Falsehood deserves correction.
The truth of Christ's death and resurrection deserves serious, faithful proclamation.
But notice the manner Peter commands.
"With meekness and fear."
The Greek πραΰτης (prautēs) conveys gentleness or meekness, while φόβος (phobos) in this context carries the sense of reverent respect.
The very verse often used to justify defending Christianity also instructs us how to conduct that defense.
Not with arrogance.
Not with contempt.
Not with a desire to crush the person asking.
But with gentleness and reverence.
And Paul gives Timothy a remarkably similar instruction.
"And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient." — 2 Timothy 2:24, KJV
Paul continues by describing correction offered with meekness, in the hope that God may grant repentance and knowledge of the truth (2 Timothy 2:25).
Read that again in your heart.
The goal of correction is not to demonstrate that we are intellectually superior.
It is to serve another person's movement toward truth.
And repentance itself is not a trophy we can force someone to hand us.
God must work in the human heart.
That changes everything about the way we speak.
Because if we truly believe the Holy Spirit transforms people, we can stop behaving as though our anger is the power that saves them.
We can be firm without being vicious.
Clear without being cruel.
Courageous without being arrogant.
And patient without compromising what Scripture teaches.
Perhaps the hardest part of this entire conversation is that many of us know these verses already.
We have read them.
We have preached them.
We have shared them.
But knowledge that never reaches our character becomes a dangerous kind of self-deception.
Jesus warned the religious leaders of His day:
"Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith." — Matthew 23:23, KJV
Jesus did not tell them to abandon obedience.
He confronted their distorted priorities.
They had become meticulous about certain religious duties while neglecting matters of profound moral importance.
Justice.
Mercy.
Faithfulness.
How easily we can repeat that pattern.
We become meticulous about doctrinal vocabulary but careless with wounded hearts.
We demand precision from strangers while excusing harshness in ourselves.
We notice the speck in another person's eye while ignoring the beam in our own, just as Jesus warned in Matthew 7:3–5.
And then we call our behavior discernment.
But discernment without humility can become suspicion.
Conviction without compassion can become cruelty.
And zeal without love can become a performance of righteousness rather than obedience to Christ.
There is a difference between standing for Jesus and using Jesus to stand above people.
One requires surrender.
The other feeds pride.
One points people toward the cross.
The other makes us the center of attention.
And if we are not careful, we can build an entire public Christian identity around winning battles while quietly losing the tenderness of our first love.
Imagine something for a moment.
A young man has spent years running from God.
His choices have left him ashamed.
He has hurt people he loves.
He has made promises he could not keep.
He knows enough about Christianity to understand that sin matters, but not enough to believe that forgiveness might still be possible for someone like him.
One night, unable to sleep, he opens his phone.
He finds a Christian post.
He reads the comments.
Believers are insulting one another.
Mocking questions.
Accusing strangers.
Competing to deliver the sharpest theological response.
He closes the app.
And in the darkness, he whispers:
"If this is what Christians are like, where would someone like me belong?"
Now imagine he finds another conversation.
The truth is still there.
Sin is not excused.
Jesus is not reduced to a symbol of vague acceptance.
But someone answers difficult questions patiently.
Someone admits when they do not know.
Someone explains repentance without humiliation.
Someone shares how Christ forgave them.
Someone treats a stranger as a person rather than an opponent.
And the young man keeps reading.
Maybe he asks a question.
Maybe someone listens.
Maybe, for the first time in years, he begins to believe that coming to Jesus is possible.
Neither imagined conversation guarantees anyone's conversion.
Only God can give new life.
But the contrast should make us ask a serious question.
When people encounter our Christianity, do they see evidence of the Savior's character, or merely the sharpness of our opinions?
Jesus said:
"By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." — John 13:35, KJV
He did not say the world would recognize His disciples because they always delivered the most devastating rebuttal.
He pointed to love.
Not love detached from obedience.
Not love that refuses to name sin.
But the self-giving love He had just commanded His disciples to show one another.
And that command becomes even more powerful when we remember what happened on the cross.
Jesus was mocked.
Rejected.
Insulted.
Crucified.
And Luke records Him saying:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." — Luke 23:34, KJV

Some early manuscripts omit this saying, a textual variation noted in modern editions. Even so, Jesus' command to love enemies and pray for persecutors is clearly established in Matthew 5:44 and Luke 6:27–28.
Consider the contrast.
We sometimes cannot endure someone disagreeing with our Facebook post without retaliating.
Yet our Lord taught His followers to love their enemies.
We sometimes refuse to forgive someone who embarrassed us.
Yet our Savior gave His life for sinners.
We sometimes treat being corrected as an unbearable insult.
Yet Jesus, who committed no sin, willingly endured humiliation for our redemption.
How can we stand at the foot of that cross and still believe that Christian maturity is measured by how effectively we embarrass people?
The cross destroys our right to boast in ourselves.
It reveals the seriousness of our sin.
It displays the depth of God's mercy.
And it calls us to die to the pride that makes every disagreement feel like a threat to our identity.
Perhaps this is why Galatians 6:1 tells spiritually mature believers to restore someone overtaken in a fault "in the spirit of meekness," while considering their own vulnerability to temptation.
Restoration.
Not entertainment.
Not public humiliation.
Not a chance to build our reputation at someone else's expense.
Restoration.
The Greek verb καταρτίζετε (katartizete), translated "restore," carries the sense of putting something right or bringing it back into proper condition.
Paul's instruction is not permission to ignore sin.
It is a call to approach a fallen person with the aim of helping them return to faithfulness.
And he warns the person doing the restoring to examine himself.
Why?
Because the one who corrects is not immune to falling.
Today you may be the one offering counsel.
Tomorrow you may be the one desperately needing mercy.
Today you may be strong in one area.
Tomorrow you may discover a weakness you never imagined.
And when that day comes, you will understand why gentleness is not weakness.
It is a gift.
Maybe you are reading this and remembering a conversation you wish you could undo.
A comment you posted.
A friend you pushed away.
A family member you corrected without listening.
A believer you judged before understanding the battle they were fighting.
Perhaps you defended a biblical position accurately, but your words carried a bitterness that had nothing to do with the Spirit of Christ.
You cannot travel backward and erase what happened.
But by God's grace, you can repent.
You can apologize without adding excuses.
You can return to that person and say:
"I still believe what Scripture teaches. But the way I treated you was wrong. I am sorry. Will you forgive me?"
Those words do not compromise biblical truth.
They demonstrate that biblical truth has begun to humble you.
And perhaps your most powerful witness will not be the argument you won.
Perhaps it will be the moment you finally admitted you were wrong.
That is not defeat.
That is repentance.
That is grace doing its transforming work.
And if you are the one who has been hurt by harsh Christians, please do not confuse the wounds inflicted by imperfect believers with the invitation of the perfect Savior.
Christ does not ask you to pretend the harm was acceptable.
He does not require you to remain in abusive situations.
Forgiveness does not eliminate the need for wisdom, accountability, or appropriate boundaries.
But He does invite you to bring your pain to Him.
To receive His mercy.
To allow His truth to heal what human pride has damaged.
And to discover that the Gospel is bigger than the failures of those who proclaim it.
There is room at the cross for the arrogant defender who needs to repent.
There is room for the wounded believer who needs healing.
There is room for the skeptic with difficult questions.
There is room for the person who has spent years hiding behind religious performance.
There is room for the sinner who finally understands that he cannot save himself.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
He died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed.
The call is not merely to become a nicer person.
It is to repent and believe the Gospel.
To surrender to Jesus Christ as Lord.
To receive His grace.
To follow Him.
And to allow His Spirit to reshape not only what we believe, but how we live.
Because a changed heart should eventually produce changed words.
Changed priorities.
Changed relationships.
Changed responses when someone disagrees.
Changed attitudes toward people we once considered beneath us.
And a growing willingness to speak the truth in love, as Ephesians 4:15 commands.
Maybe the next time you encounter someone who disagrees with your faith, you will still explain what you believe.
You should.
But perhaps you will listen first.
Perhaps you will ask a sincere question.
Perhaps you will refuse to mock.
Perhaps you will recognize when a conversation is no longer fruitful.
Perhaps you will choose prayer over another angry reply.
Perhaps you will remember that the person in front of you is not merely an argument to defeat.
They are a human being made in the image of God.
Someone with a story.
Someone with fears.
Someone with wounds you may never see.
Someone who needs the truth.
Someone who needs the love of Christ.
Just as you do.
And perhaps, when that moment comes, the Holy Spirit will bring one question back to your heart:
"Am I trying to win this person to my side, or am I faithfully pointing this person toward Jesus?"
That question may change the way you speak.
It may change the way you post.
It may change the way you parent.
It may change the way you correct your spouse.
It may change the way you respond to someone who has disappointed you.
It may even change the way you understand spiritual maturity.
Because maturity in Christ is not simply knowing more verses than someone else.
It is growing in the likeness of the One those verses reveal.
And the more clearly we see Him, the less room there should be for self-righteous pride.
Not whether you agree with this article.
Not whether you can think of five Christians who need to read it.
But whether the Holy Spirit has brought anything in your own heart to light.
Have you been more concerned about being right than being loving?
Have you remained silent about truth because you were afraid of rejection?
Have you been wounded by someone who claimed to speak for God?
Or have you been trying to find your way back to Jesus after years of disappointment?
You do not need to pretend here.
If you are still healing from the way others treated you, you can comment, "Christ is still healing me."

You do not owe strangers the details of your pain. But sometimes a small, honest sentence becomes the beginning of a meaningful conversation, a prayer, or the encouragement another struggling believer needs.
And please, do not let this message end with you.
Not to shame another Christian.
Not to settle an old argument.
But to help bring our attention back to Jesus.
Because we all need reminders.
Especially when our pride starts speaking louder than our faith.
And if this kind of Scripture-centered reflection has encouraged you, I would love for you to stay connected with Gospel Warrior.

We want Gospel Warrior to remain a place where people can encounter biblical truth, thoughtful correction, spiritual encouragement, honest conversations about repentance, and the life-changing hope of Jesus Christ.
It is a practical way to partner with this ministry's mission.
Scripture encourages generous support for Gospel ministry (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14), while also teaching that giving should be willing, not pressured or reluctant (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Your local church, family responsibilities, and existing commitments matter.
Think of it as a recurring ministry-support offering if that is how you prayerfully choose to give—not as a required biblical tithe or a replacement for responsibilities to your local congregation.
It is the opportunity to participate in making Christ-centered encouragement and discipleship resources available to others.
A simple share may reach someone we could never reach personally.
A friend who has stopped praying.
A believer who has become bitter.
A parent who needs to apologize.
A young person who believes Christianity is nothing more than judgment.
A wounded soul who needs to hear that Jesus Christ still calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His finished work.
We cannot know what God may do through one faithful act of encouragement.
But we can choose to make the message available.
And that is why this mission matters.
Not because Gospel Warrior deserves the spotlight.
Not because any writer, page, or ministry can change a human heart.
Only Christ saves.
Only His Gospel reconciles sinners to God.
Only His Spirit produces lasting spiritual transformation.
We are simply seeking to point people toward Him.
And if the day ever comes when this ministry becomes more concerned about winning attention than faithfully representing Jesus, then we too must return to the very message we are sharing today.
Because none of us is above the call to repentance.
Not the preacher.
Not the writer.
Not the apologist.
Not the person who shares this article.
And certainly not the person who wrote it.
We all stand in need of the same grace.
So let us be Christians who know what we believe and why we believe it.
Let us study Scripture carefully.
Let us defend the Gospel faithfully.
Let us refuse to compromise biblical truth.
But let us also be people who listen.
People who weep with those who weep.
People who restore the fallen with gentleness.
People who confess when we have sinned.
People whose courage is shaped by humility.
People who remember that Jesus did not call us merely to win arguments.
He called us to follow Him.
And following Him will sometimes mean standing firmly when the world disagrees.
Sometimes it will mean speaking an uncomfortable truth.
Sometimes it will mean walking away from a pointless quarrel.
And sometimes it will mean looking someone in the eyes and saying:
"I was wrong. Please forgive me."
That, too, can glorify God.
Because the Gospel does not merely change the destination of those who belong to Christ.
It transforms the way we walk.
The way we speak.
The way we love.
The way we forgive.
And the way we treat the very people who disagree with us.
One day, the comments will be forgotten.
The arguments will be buried beneath thousands of other conversations.
The applause will fade.
The online victories will mean very little.
But the love we showed, the truth we spoke faithfully, the apologies we offered, and the people we helped point toward Jesus will not have been wasted.
So before you write your next reply, ask yourself one final question.
If someone learned what Jesus is like only by watching the way I treat people, what kind of Savior would they think I follow?
May our lives give them a reason to look beyond us and see Him.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be losing an argument about Jesus.
It would be winning the argument while refusing to live like someone who has been changed by His grace.
The world may forget the argument you won, but a wounded soul may remember for years whether your words made it easier or harder to hear the invitation of Jesus.
